talks.title: Google Maps Hacks
talks.teaser: Artist Simon Weckert explains how wheeling 99 smartphones in a handcart generated virtual traffic jams in Google Maps.
talks.summary:
Artist and technologist Simon Weckert presents his world-renowned hack on Google Maps navigation systems. By transporting 99 secondhand smartphones running navigation apps in a handcart through central Berlin, he demonstrated how digital geospatial algorithms can be manipulated to produce physical impacts in the real world.

Weckert reviews the methodology behind generating virtual traffic congestion, explaining how Google Maps aggregated location telemetry from his concentrated cluster of slow-moving phones to falsely conclude a severe traffic jam was underway. He shows how the algorithm turned green streets bright red on map interfaces and automatically rerouted real vehicular traffic onto other streets, prompting a wider discussion on society's dependency on opaque algorithmic systems.

talks.title: Pickpocketing at Home
talks.teaser: Explores the psychological mechanics of theatrical pickpocketing, misdirection cues, and physical spatial awareness.
talks.summary:
Magician, physical security specialist, and entertainer James Harrison leads an engaging instructional session in the Rogues Village on the mechanics, psychology, and physical techniques of pickpocketing that practitioners can practice at home [00:04]. Harrison explains that pickpocketing relies heavily on social engineering, situational awareness, and psychological misdirection rather than superhuman sleight of hand [06:06].

Harrison breaks down the anatomy of a theft, explaining how pickpockets case crowds to identify vulnerable targets—specifically individuals who readily accept people entering their personal space and follow verbal instructions [06:06]. He details a practical home training setup, demonstrating how hanging a hoodie or winter jacket from a doorframe using a hanger allows practitioners to develop muscle memory and calibrate physical touch sensitivity [12:17]. He illustrates techniques for dipping into "quick pockets" (such as exterior jacket pockets and front hoodie pouches) to extract dummy wallets, smartphones, and keycards without alerting the wearer [19:16].

The presentation explores sensory manipulation and visual sightlines, showing how executing movements directly beneath a target's chin or outside their peripheral vision renders physical contact undetectable [26:35]. Harrison demonstrates how physical anchors—such as guiding someone's shoulder or pointing toward a distant object—saturate the brain's sensory bandwidth and mask simultaneous pocket extractions [33:45].
